Round 13 — the hero media column: what the plate and the mark each get

A2 puts a Byrne Euclid leaf in PS-1 and a 1910 geometry plate in PS-3 (D149-1b/2b). PS-1 already holds the club's mark, and the column is a row: put a plate in it and the two graphics split the column's width. Measured on the built page with the real plate in it, the mark falls from 376×235 to 188×118 and its thinnest stroke lands at 1.02px against D119's 1px floor, while the plate becomes a 188×125 window on a 688×1004 leaf that keeps only 46% of itself. With the hatched placeholder box the review build stands in for — the state every earlier measurement of this defect used — the column falls to 152×95 and check:render prints 7 FAILs. So the question is not whether a gate goes red: it is what the column holds. It is laid out here as pictures of the real page with the real art in it — every number on this page was produced by the gates, and nothing in it is transcribed by hand.

measured 2026-11-03 21:21 on the review build (siteFp 7cb0444724); the shipped page for comparison is siteFp 00adf2c64c. The column as built

PS-1 is 376×574 at 840,200 at 1240 — the 574px is the row's height, which the text column beside it already pays for. The mark at full column width paints 376×235 (viewBox 240×150, so every stroke is 1.3 viewBox units at scale 1.57). That leaves 307px of a column the page is already paying for.

The two states split the column differently because a hatched box and an inline image are flex items with different intrinsic sizes — 149×93 against 188×118 — and only the placeholder state fails the floor outright. The real-image state is legal at 1240 by a hundredth of a pixel, which is a fact about the arithmetic rather than an endorsement: at that size the plate is a postage stamp on a portrait leaf and the mark is the smallest drawing the rules allow. Instrument note, measured on this branch. The gate used to assert D119's 1px floor on every shape's stroke-width, including the mark's meeting point — a filled disc styled stroke-none, whose stroke-width is the SVG initial value of 1 and which paints no stroke at all. Below a drawn scale of 1.0 that phantom shape failed, so one of the eight FAILs earlier sessions quoted was arithmetic about a stroke that does not exist. The floor is now asserted on a stroke that paints (strokePaints, from the same computed style), and check:render:selftest gained the counterfactual — give that disc a real 0.3-unit stroke and the gate fails it like any line. The FAILs quoted above are painted strokes, one each.

Two probes, two numbers, both right. On the same planted review build, check:space puts the mark at 152×95 and check:render at 148.9×93.1: the gate runs in a viewport with a vertical scrollbar, which steals about 10px of width from a centred column. Every stroke figure in this specimen is arithmetic on the gate's box, because that is the box the gate measures and the smaller of the two.

What "covered" means. The vertical run of one meridian was scanned in the live page at device resolution, pixel by pixel, against the ground the mark actually stands on (the modal colour inside the mark's own box — measured, not assumed: 94.80% of that box is paper). Distance is measured in OKLab, the space check:color and check:ground already use. A pixel of the mark's token on this ground reads 0.667 when it fully covers its pixel — that is the ceiling. Coverage is the strongest pixel the line reaches divided by that ceiling. A stroke set at less than a whole device pixel splits its colour across two of them and never reaches full ink; that is what the coverage figure shows, which makes D119's coverage claim a measurement rather than an assertion.

What the art costs the palette. "page colour" is the share of the whole page at chroma ≥ 0.08, the quantity check:color enforces (reading bar: 33% of any named family). The page today is 0.01%; a Byrne leaf in the column takes it to 0.09% in the row and 0.30% stacked, because flat engraving is nearly all paper. Every option stays two orders of magnitude under the bar; the figure is here so that "add the art" has its cost written next to its picture.

The plate's shape is part of the question

The leaf is 688×1004 — a portrait. D149-1b/2b: the operator's pick for PS-1 — Euclid in flat colour, drawn with the same lines, arcs and right angles as our own mark. A 3:2 box (what the markup reserves today) keeps 46% of it; the column's own leftover keeps 56%; the column at the plate's own shape keeps all of it. Cropping is a claim about the page, so it is drawn at true size:

The screenshots below are 1:1 at 1240. The plate column is what the crop keeps of the 688×1004 leaf and how much of the crop is chromatic enough to name. The mark column is measured three ways, and they are not the same claim: set is the stroke's device width the markup asks for (the geometry table's viewBox units × the box scale — what the gate rules on against D119's 1px floor, and the cell is shaded where it is under it); ink is the width of the painted run across the mark's one vertical stroke, which includes antialiased pixels and so reads ~1px wider; covered is how close the strongest pixel of that run comes to full coverage of the token it is painted with, measured against the ground the mark actually sits on — D119's actual claim is about coverage, and this is the only one of the three that tests it. check:render is the real gate run on that variant.

What the plates do to the page's colour

D119 counts the page at chroma ≥ 0.08, and the attention bar is where that count is enforced. The shipped page sits at 0.01%; every option below is measured by check:color on the built page, not predicted from the crop. Against the shipped page, the Byrne leaf costs 0.41% at most and 0.07% at least — the difference between the options is how much leaf is on screen, so the — empty attention cell is not the thing that changes.

The join section's plate (not a question — a confirmation)

D149-2b ruled the 1910 Euler plate into PS-3 at 526×316. Since then the two join actions moved outside the tinted card (D149-3c), so that column is now 532×56 inside a grid row the copy column already makes 326px tall. The ruled plate is 532×316, keeps 84% of a 698×350 leaf, and in option G the page measures 4327px with the plate inside the row it belongs to — it costs +43px of height. Source: Plane geometry, with problems and applications (Slaught & Lennes, 1910).

Questions

Q1 — which composition?

Answer with the letter. A = the plate as ruled, in the column exactly as built (this is what A2 ships today) · B = stack the column; plate keeps the 3:2 ratio in the markup · C = stack the column; the plate takes everything the mark does not need · D = the plate keeps its own shape at full width; the mark shrinks to the smallest legal size · E = the plate owns PS-1; the mark moves to the words · F = leave the row, pin the mark’s stroke to device pixels · G = the stacked column at its leftover size, plus the PS-3 plate exactly as D149-2b ruled it

Recommendation: C. the column is exactly full (plate + gap + mark = the 574px the row already costs). check:render on it: green at 1240, 640, 390, 320 (mark 376×235, thinnest stroke 2.04 computed / 3px of solid ink, floor 1px). It costs the page +0px of height, and it gives the art more of the column than B, which keeps 46% of the leaf instead of 56%. If the art matters more than the mark's size, E keeps the plate whole and puts a 240×150 mark beside the club's name instead — strokes 1.3px, and +170px of page.

F exists to show what pinning the stroke does, measured against A at the identical size (both 188×118): the ink run across the mark's vertical meridian is 2px pinned vs 2px scaled, and its strongest pixel covers 100% of the ground against 91% — so vector-effect: non-scaling-stroke does put more paint where the arithmetic says there is barely any, which is exactly what the gate cannot see: it computes 1.02 for both, because it multiplies viewBox units by the box scale and does not know about vector-effect. Choosing it means changing a gate rule as well as the markup — and the mark is still a 188×118 drawing.

Q2 — PS-4, the event-card thumb: art or no art?

The slot is defined but not built (src/assets/photos/README.md: 323×110 inside the measured card; the event sections are switched off until A6 gives them real dates). Record 0023 measured the only plate wide enough for a thumb: Byrne 123-184 keeps 93% of itself in the box and would add +0.032% to the whole page at chroma ≥ 0.08 — an order of magnitude below what PS-1 costs. So a thumb is cheap and a void is avoidable.

Answer: (a) art in the thumb when a plate fits it, (b) no art in PS-4 — text-only cards.

How to read the pictures: they are screenshots of the built page at 1240, cropped from the top of the hero grid to its bottom, so the geometry in the picture is the geometry the probe reported. On a narrow screen the browser scales the picture down; compare the boxes and the numbers, not the pixels. Answer in letter form (e.g. “1c, 2a”).
